title: Berkshire 1981: Why buy 10% of a wonderful business over 100% at double
summary: Buffett explains why he prefers fractional stakes in great businesses to costly control deals, why high-premium takeovers rarely work, and how rising passive interest rates erode the value of ordinary equity. He also covers insurance underwriting discipline and float-driven pricing pressure.

principles.text: Prefer a small slice of a wonderful business at a fair price over owning all of it at double.
principles.quote: we would rather buy 10% of Wonderful Business T at X per share than 100% of T at 2X per share.

principles.text: Acquisition premiums are driven by ego, size obsession and kiss-the-toad optimism, not by economics.
principles.quote: investors can always buy toads at the going price for toads. If investors instead bankroll princesses who wish to pay double for the right to kiss the toad, those kisses had better pack some real dynamite.

principles.text: Optimize for real economic benefit, not size or reported accounting numbers.
principles.quote: Our acquisition decisions will be aimed at maximizing real economic benefits, not at maximizing either managerial domain or reported numbers for accounting purposes.

principles.text: Buy fractional stakes in businesses with excellent franchises and competent, honest managers; don't plan to run them.
principles.quote: Currently, we find values most easily obtained through the open-market purchase of fractional positions in companies with excellent business franchises and competent, honest managements.

principles.text: High-return businesses should retain earnings; low-return ones should pay them out so owners can redeploy capital.
principles.quote: Logically, a company with historic and prospective high returns on equity should retain much or all of its earnings so that shareholders can earn premium returns on enhanced capital.

principles.text: Insurers desperate for cash flow price business at any price; discipline means turning down volume.
principles.quote: Such insurers necessarily fear a major decrease in volume more than they fear a major underwriting loss.
